purpose: Specify mixing methods, order of operations, fermentation/proof endpoints, doneness signal hierarchy, and failure diagnosis/recovery so baking execution is controlled and diagnosable.
assumptions: home or small-batch equipment with variable ambient temperature
an instant-read thermometer is preferred when available but not always present
product-class style intent is known or elicited (fudgy vs cakey, lean vs enriched)
exclusions: professional pastry competition judging rubrics as law
meat/poultry food-safety cooking as primary scope (escalate if asked as safety authority)

competency_questions.question: Which mixing method and order of operations should this product use?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names method family and critical order constraints

competency_questions.question: What are the critical temperature and order constraints during mix (yeast liquid bands, chocolate working temps, fat plasticity, egg temper)?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: lists applicable numeric bands: active dry rehydrate ~40–43 °C; instant with dough ~24–27 °C; yeast death ~54–60 °C; chocolate work ~31–32 °C dark / ~29–30 °C milk-white; plus egg temper and fat plasticity cues

competency_questions.question: How do you execute creaming vs muffin vs biscuit methods without breaking emulsion or overmixing?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states endpoints and main failure mode for the chosen method

competency_questions.question: How do you build and protect a foam sponge structure through fold?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: defines foam stage and fold rules that preserve volume

competency_questions.question: How is gluten development and fermentation endpoint judged for this dough?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: gives development test and proof endpoint not only clock time

competency_questions.question: What controls oven spring and how should heat/steam be managed?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: links proof state, scoring/steam if relevant, and early heat

competency_questions.question: When and how must eggs, chocolate, or hot liquids be tempered?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names temper protocol for the relevant system

competency_questions.question: What is the doneness signal hierarchy for this product?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: orders signals and cites temp target if any

competency_questions.question: How do you resolve dark crust with unset center?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: uses hierarchy: tent/lower heat, trust temp/structure over color

competency_questions.question: How should skewer, color, and touch be interpreted for this style?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: style-specific interpretation rules stated under hierarchy

competency_questions.question: What caused sunk center, dense crumb, or tough/dry texture, and what is the primary fix?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: differential diagnosis with one primary cause and matched fix

competency_questions.question: What can be recovered in-process versus what requires restart, and what preflight prevents it next time?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: classifies actionable vs terminal and lists prevention updates

glossary.definition: Beating plastic fat with sugar to trap air and build a light emulsion base
Two-bowl wet/dry mix combined briefly to minimize gluten development
Stretching a dough film thin enough to transmit light without tearing; marks strong gluten development
Finger poke on proofing dough; slow spring-back indicates ready proof for many breads
Rapid final rise in the oven from gas expansion before structure sets
Ordered preference of internal temp, structural probes, touch, then color
Continued temperature rise and cooking from residual heat after removal from oven
Firming of starch gels, foams, or chocolate as product cools after bake or melt
Fermentation past gas-retention capacity leading to collapse risk in the oven
Egg-sugar foam falling from a whisk in a slowly dissolving ribbon; foam readiness cue

source_registry.description: heuristic prior estimates for culinary_technique_doneness work units in absence of supplied datasets
source_registry.citation_or_locator: heuristic prior; no external dataset supplied

nodes.definition: Define the legal order of combining ingredients for the chosen method: when salt meets yeast, when liquids meet flour, when leavener meets wet acid, when chocolate melts into batter. Order errors cause premature chemical reaction, gluten overdevelopment, or broken emulsions before technique details matter.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: method family change (cream vs muffin) rewrites legal order

pros.claim: Correct order preserves leavening gas and emulsion for the whole bake window
pros.example: adding powder into dry flour before wet mix delays reaction vs dumping powder into buttermilk first

cons.claim: Some modern reverse-creaming orders intentionally break classic sequence
cons.example: high-ratio cakes may mix fat into flour first

failure_modes: wetting baking powder then delaying oven by an hour
adding flour all at once to whipped egg foam deflating it
acceptance_tests: written order of operations matches chosen method family

nodes.definition: Beat plastic fat with sugar to pale and fluffy, trapping air cells, then add eggs gradually to maintain emulsion, then dry ingredients. Fat must be plastic (~65 F / 18 C butter), not melted. Used for many cookies and butter cakes. Stop when specified stage reaches; overcream can warm fat and collapse structure.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: fat type not plastic at room conditions or mixer power changes stage timing

pros.claim: Creaming builds the primary air skeleton chemical leavening later expands
pros.example: properly creamed pound cake batter lightens in color and volume before flour

cons.claim: Warm kitchens melt butter mid-cream causing grease-out
cons.example: summer kitchens need chill pauses

failure_modes: using melted butter in a creaming recipe
adding all eggs at once splitting batter
acceptance_tests: fat plasticity confirmed; stage cue documented; emulsion intact after eggs

nodes.definition: Mix dry ingredients in one bowl, wet in another (oil or melted fat OK), combine briefly until just moistened. Lumps OK; overmix develops gluten and tunnels. Ideal for muffins, many quick breads, and oil cakes. Chemical leavener is typical; bake soon after mix.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: baker overmixes from habit of smooth batter aesthetics

pros.claim: Short mix keeps crumb tender and open for oil-based batters
pros.example: blueberry muffins with 10-12 stirs stay tender

cons.claim: Undermixing can leave flour pockets
cons.example: streaks of dry flour in loaf

failure_modes: whisking muffin batter until perfectly smooth
holding mixed batter hours before bake
acceptance_tests: mix endpoint is just-moistened; bake window stated

nodes.definition: Cut cold solid fat into flour to pea/crumb sizes, then add cold liquid minimally. Steam from fat pieces lifts layers. Keep fat solid; overwork after liquid makes tough biscuits. Related to pie dough with tighter hydration control.

excluded: yeasted laminated croissant full protocol detail as primary

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: fat temperature rises above plasticity window during cut-in

pros.claim: Visible fat pieces create steam lift and flaky layers
pros.example: pea-sized butter in biscuits yields separation

cons.claim: Too-large fat chunks leave greasy holes; too-fine resembles shortbread mealy dough
cons.example: over-processed food processor dough

failure_modes: using soft warm butter
kneading biscuit dough like bread
acceptance_tests: fat remains cool and particulate; dough not elastic-smooth

nodes.definition: Whip eggs (whole, yolks, or whites) with sugar to ribbon or soft/firm peaks, then fold dry ingredients and optional melted butter gently. Structure is protein foam + starch set; deflation is the main risk. Genoise, biscuit cuillère, angel food variants differ in fat and white handling.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: egg temperature or whip stage target changes foam stability

pros.claim: Foam methods achieve lift with little or no chemical leavener when foam is stable
pros.example: genoise volume from whole-egg foam ribbon stage

cons.claim: humidity, fat traces on bowls, and overfold kill foam volume irreversibly; grease contamination is a common terminal failure for angel food
cons.example: genoise loses 30%+ volume from aggressive flour fold; angel food collapses if tools have residual butter

failure_modes: stirring flour into foam vigorously instead of folding
adding hot melted butter in one pour to a whole-egg foam
opening the oven early on a soufflé or angel food before structure sets
acceptance_tests: foam stage defined with visual/tactile cue
fold protocol protects volume
revisit_triggers: egg size or temp process change

nodes.definition: Apply mechanical energy (hand, mixer, stretch-and-fold) until dough passes product-class window tests (windowpane for strong bread; shorter for pizza/crackers). Autolyse and rest reduce knead energy. Underdeveloped dough cannot retain gas; overdeveloped dough tears and bakes tight.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: flour protein change alters time-to-windowpane

pros.claim: Correct development maximizes gas retention for open crumb
pros.example: windowpane on baguette dough predicts oven spring potential

cons.claim: High-hydration doughs develop with folds better than intense early kneading
cons.example: ciabatta slapped too early becomes sticky mess

failure_modes: kneading enriched dough to bread windowpane destroying butter emulsion
fixed 10-minute mix ignoring dough feel
acceptance_tests: development endpoint named for product class with test

nodes.definition: Folding incorporates flour into foams or builds layered strength in doughs without degassing fully. For batters: cut through center, scoop, turn bowl. For bread: stretch-and-fold during bulk. Laminated pastry is a specialized fold/roll fat-lock protocol — call out when full lamination is required vs simple folds.

included: when to escalate to full lamination protocol

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: operator aggressiveness causes foam loss or butter breakout in lamination

pros.claim: Gentle folds preserve foam or build strength with less tearing
pros.example: three folds during bulk improve dough strength at 75% hydration

cons.claim: Underfolding leaves flour lumps; overfolding deflates sponge
cons.example: genoise sinks 30% from aggressive fold

failure_modes: using a mixer on high to 'fold'
rolling laminated dough warm until butter leaks
acceptance_tests: fold style matched to foam vs dough context

nodes.definition: Schedule bench rest, bulk fermentation, and final proof with endpoints by volume, jiggly feel, or poke test — not clock alone. Temperature logs convert time. Retardation in cold slows yeast for flavor and schedule control. Underproof collapses less but stays dense; overproof collapses in oven.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: ambient temperature swings invalidate fixed minute schedules

pros.claim: Endpoint-based proofing adapts to kitchen temperature
pros.example: poke spring-back slow at 24 C means ready even if clock is early

cons.claim: enriched doughs proof slower and mask visual cues under fat and sugar so clock-only schedules under- or overproof across seasons
cons.example: brioche looks small yet is ready by poke feel; winter kitchen underproofs a fixed 60-minute bulk

failure_modes: proofing every product to 'double' blindly regardless of enrichment
baking a severely overproofed loaf without a reshape decision
using wall-clock minutes alone when ambient temperature swung 8 °C
acceptance_tests: proof endpoint is volume/feel/poke not only minutes
temperature assumption recorded

nodes.definition: Temper by gradually equalizing temperatures: hot milk into yolks for custard; cool chocolate through crystal stages for snap/shine; warm liquids into the yeast-safe band. Numeric bands: active dry yeast rehydrate about 40–43 °C (105–110 °F); instant yeast usually direct-added with dough target about 24–27 °C; yeast stress/degradation begins near ~46 °C and death around ~54–60 °C. Chocolate working temps roughly ~31–32 °C dark and ~29–30 °C milk/white for tempered coatings. Thermal shock curdles eggs, loses chocolate temper, or kills yeast.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: induction heat speed or chocolate couverture type changes temper window

pros.claim: Tempering prevents curdled pastry cream and dull soft chocolate coatings
pros.example: ladle hot milk into yolks while whisking before returning to pot

cons.claim: home chocolate temper without a thermometer is unreliable in hot rooms; induction heat can overshoot yolk and yeast bands quickly
cons.example: seized chocolate from a steam drop; yolks scrambled by dumping all hot milk at once; instant yeast killed by 60 °C liquid

failure_modes: pouring all hot milk into yolks at once scrambles them
working chocolate above ~32 °C loses temper and soft snap
hydrating active dry yeast well above 43 °C or killing any yeast near 54–60 °C
acceptance_tests: temper steps present for custard/chocolate/yeast-hot-liquid paths
yeast liquid and dough temperature bands stated with numbers when yeast is used
chocolate working temperature band stated when tempering coatings
custard yolk temper steps present when hot dairy meets eggs

nodes.definition: Rank doneness signals: (1) internal temperature for products with known targets, (2) structural probes (skewer/toothpick with product-class interpretation), (3) spring-back touch, (4) visual color/crust — never color alone for high-sugar or deep pans. Hierarchy resolves conflicting signals (dark top, wet center).

excluded: sensory tasting notes as only criterion

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: product class without reliable temp target needs alternate top signals documented

pros.claim: Hierarchy prevents pulling on color while center is unset
pros.example: bread at 96-99 C internal despite pale crust in steamed oven

cons.claim: some confections set primarily on cool (cheesecake jiggle then chill) so hot-out-of-oven hierarchy must include cool-set exceptions
cons.example: cheesecake judged done only when hot and firm overbakes; molten cake judged by clean skewer destroys style

failure_modes: using only toothpick rules on molten-center desserts
declaring done on crust color alone for deep or high-sugar products
ignoring temperature when a calibrated probe and target exist
acceptance_tests: hierarchy ordered and product-class exceptions noted
internal temp used when a target exists
revisit_triggers: repeated sunk centers after color-based pulls

nodes.definition: Maintain a table of internal temperature targets for probe-at-thickest-center (avoid pan metal): lean bread ~96–99 °C; enriched bread often slightly lower by style; butter and sponge cakes ~93–99 °C (200–210 °F); cheesecake center ~65–70 °C (then cool-set finishes the slice); intentionally under-set styles such as molten or fudgy centers ~71–77 °C; custards roughly ~76–82 °C depending on style. Temperature dominates color when both are available. Poultry/meat safety endpoints are out of primary scope.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: probe calibration drift or target table revision

pros.claim: Numeric center temp removes most guesswork for breads and many cakes
pros.example: pull sandwich loaf at ~94-96 C for slightly softer crumb if style wants

cons.claim: wrong table row ruins style — molten cakes and fudgy brownies intentionally pull below dry-skewer cake temps; cheesecake is not a bread target
cons.example: applying 99 °C bread pull to a lava cake; using bread temps on cheesecake instead of 65–70 °C center plus chill set

failure_modes: probe hitting pan floor reading high
applying bread temps to custard or cheesecake
omitting cake and cheesecake rows so color becomes the default stop rule
acceptance_tests: target temperature listed for product when applicable
probe placement avoids pan metal
target temperature listed for product when applicable including cake and cheesecake rows when relevant

nodes.definition: Insert skewer in center: wet batter = underdone for set cakes; few moist crumbs often OK for tender cakes; totally dry can mean overbake. Molten-center desserts reverse the rule. Skewer is secondary to temperature when both apply.

included: wet vs moist crumb vs clean

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: product style (fudgy vs cakey) changes crumb interpretation

pros.claim: Skewer gives fast center moisture read without a thermometer
pros.example: toothpick with moist crumbs on butter cake often perfect

cons.claim: Chocolate and fruit wet the skewer even when set
cons.example: false underdone reads

failure_modes: demanding bone-dry skewer on all cakes
using skewer alone on deep dense fruitcake without time
acceptance_tests: interpretation rule stated for the product style

nodes.definition: Crust color indicates Maillard/caramel progress and surface dryness, not center set. Use to modulate heat (tent with foil, lower rack) while center finishes. Pale weak crust can still house a set crumb; dark crust can hide raw centers.

included: rank below temp and structure probes

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: oven hot spots or sugar budget change color curve

pros.claim: Reading color as a control lever not a stop rule saves high-sugar cakes
pros.example: foil tent when mahogany while center still lags 5 C

cons.claim: Steam-injected ovens keep crust pale until late
cons.example: bakers used to home dry ovens misread

failure_modes: pulling solely because color matches a photo
ignoring burning edges while waiting for photo color on top
acceptance_tests: color used to adjust heat not to alone declare done

nodes.definition: Light center press: cake should spring back with slight imprint for many butter cakes; cheesecake retains a designed jiggle band; bread loaf sides feel set. Touch is tertiary and burns risk — use thoughtfully. Jiggle charts are product-specific.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: product style changes spring vs jiggle targets

pros.claim: Spring-back catches soft underbake when thermometer unavailable
pros.example: center imprint that stays deep means more time

cons.claim: Gloved touch is dull; bare touch risks burns
cons.example: hot sugar surfaces

failure_modes: pressing foam cakes hard deflating them
expecting bread poke test identical to cake spring
acceptance_tests: touch cue defined per product if used

nodes.definition: Sunken center after bake or cool: causes include underbake (unset starch/protein), excess leavener (rise then collapse), overproof, premature oven opening, excess sugar/fat delaying set, or cooling shock. Diagnosis order: was center set at pull? was rise excessive then fall? did it sink on cool only?

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: repeated sink pattern suggests systematic formula or process cause

pros.claim: Differentiating underbake from collapse selects opposite fixes (more time vs less leavener)
pros.example: wet skewer sink → bake longer; dry skewer dome-crater → reduce powder or proof

cons.claim: multiple causes can co-occur (overproof plus underbake) so single-lever shotgun fixes hide the primary cause
cons.example: wet skewer sink needs more time; dry-skewer dome-crater needs less leavener or less proof — opposite fixes

failure_modes: always adding flour after any sink without reading signals
always reducing sugar first without diagnosis
changing leavener, time, and hydration in one trial so the next bake is uninterpretable
acceptance_tests: diagnostic tree applied with signal evidence
fix targets distinct causes not shotgun changes

nodes.definition: Dense crumb: underdevelopment, underproof, weak leavener, excess liquid without structure, overmix tunneling extremes, or wrong flour protein. Distinguish tight even dense (underproof/underleaven) from gummy dense (underbake/enzyme/hydration). Fixes differ.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: user describes density without crumb photo or process notes

pros.claim: Splitting gummy vs tight density avoids wrong flour dumps
pros.example: gummy → bake/set/hydration; tight → proof/yeast/development

cons.claim: Enrichment naturally denser crumb than lean baguette; expectation mismatch
cons.example: brioche judged by ciabatta standard

failure_modes: adding random oil to fix density
always doubling yeast
acceptance_tests: density type classified before fix

nodes.definition: Tough: excess gluten development, low fat/sugar, overbake, or high protein flour in tender product. Dry: overbake, low fat/sugar/water, or stale storage. Separate toughness (chewy resistance) from dryness (low moisture perception).

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: overmix habit or oven runs hot

pros.claim: Naming tough vs dry picks method fix vs bake-time fix
pros.example: tough muffins → less mix; dry muffins → less time or more fat/sugar/water

cons.claim: Staling (starch retrogradation) mimics dry bake errors next day
cons.example: day-2 dry is storage not always bake

failure_modes: brushing water on tough crust expecting tenderness inside
reducing bake blindly when toughness is gluten
acceptance_tests: tough vs dry labeled with process evidence

nodes.definition: Recovery moves when still actionable: reshape overproofed dough if strength remains; chill spread-prone cookie dough; re-emulsify split batter with flour spoonful; extend bake when skewer wet and top not burning; tent color while center finishes. Know non-recoverable states (burnt, curdled solid, fully collapsed foam).

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: new failure mode without recovery playbook entry

pros.claim: Early recovery saves batches that rigid recipes would scrap
pros.example: wet center + settable top → lower heat and extend rather than bin

cons.claim: recovery can produce non-original quality and must be disclosed; terminal states (burnt, fully collapsed foam, killed yeast) should not be sold as the original product
cons.example: reshaped overproof loaf is denser; collapsed angel food cannot be whipped back to full volume

failure_modes: microwaving a raw-center cake as the primary recovery for guests
whipping a fully collapsed angel food expecting original volume
proceeding with greasy broken batter without a re-emulsify attempt or restart decision
acceptance_tests: actionable vs terminal classification made
recovery play matched to diagnosis

nodes.definition: During creaming and high-fat mixes, watch for emulsion integrity: smooth glossy batter vs curdled separated look. Temperature and addition rate are controls. Links technique to fat/egg systems without redoing full chemistry KB.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: kitchen temperature or butter brand water content changes emulsion ease

pros.claim: Catching split early enables recovery before flour locks the break
pros.example: stop adding eggs; warm bowl slightly; beat in spoon of flour

cons.claim: Some high-ratio methods look loosely emulsified yet bake fine
cons.example: appearance alone can false-alarm

failure_modes: continuing to add liquid to a badly split base without intervention
baking greasy broken batter as-is without attempt
acceptance_tests: emulsion status checked at egg and liquid addition stages

nodes.definition: Before mix: confirm method, ingredient temps, leavener freshness, pan prep, oven preheat and rack position, timer and probe ready, order of operations card. Prevention is cheaper than diagnosis. Preflight checklist is mandatory for high-risk foam and custard work.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: checklist skip correlates with failure reports

pros.claim: Preflight removes the most common process failures before they start
pros.example: cold butter for biscuits checked before flour weighed

cons.claim: Overlong checklists get skipped entirely
cons.example: must stay short and high-leverage

failure_modes: starting foam with greasy bowl
opening oven every 2 minutes from anxiety without plan
acceptance_tests: preflight completed for method and doneness tools

nodes.definition: Many products finish structure on cooling: starch gel firms, foams stabilize, chocolate sets, cookies crisp. Unmold timing, rack cooling vs in-pan, and humidity affect final texture. Pulling evaluation only at hot-out-of-oven misjudges set and sink.

excluded: blast freezer industrial cycles as primary

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: unmold timing or room humidity changes cool-set outcomes

pros.claim: Evaluating after cool prevents false underdone calls and explains cool-sinks
pros.example: cheesecake set judged after chill not at jiggly hot pull alone

cons.claim: Some products must be served warm and never reach full cool set
cons.example: molten cake intentional

failure_modes: forcing unmold of fragile hot sponge
wrapping hot bread trapping steam sogging crust
acceptance_tests: cool protocol and evaluation time stated

nodes.definition: Oven spring is the final rapid rise from gas expansion and residual yeast before set. Needs score (for bread), sufficient proof not overproof, and adequate early heat. Steam delays crust set for spring. Heat profile (front-load high then lower) is a technique lever tied to doneness hierarchy.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: oven preheat inadequacy or steam practice change

pros.claim: Managing spring improves volume without changing formula chemistry
pros.example: preheated stone + steam boost baguette spring

cons.claim: Excess early heat sets crust too fast trapping raw center risk in large loaves
cons.example: burnt crust underdone crumb

failure_modes: loading cold oven for yeast bread expecting spring
scoring after spring already done
acceptance_tests: spring plan matches proof state and oven prep
revisit_triggers: flat loaves with good proof notes

nodes.definition: Residual heat continues to cook centers after pull — larger roasts more than small cookies, but dense loaves and custards also carry over. Pull slightly before final temp target when carryover is material. Resting equalizes temperature and finishes set for some products.

excluded: large animal butchery carryover beyond baking scope

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: loaf size or pull temperature habit change

pros.claim: Accounting carryover reduces dry overbaked centers
pros.example: pull custard at slight jiggle knowing chill sets remainder

cons.claim: Tiny cookies have negligible carryover; applying roast rules overpulls underdone
cons.example: wrong scale application

failure_modes: waiting for max temp on every product ignoring carryover
slicing bread steaming-hot destroying crumb
acceptance_tests: carryover considered when mass is large or custard-style

touch is a lower-ranked signal

conflict_axes.name: color_aesthetics_vs_center_set
conflict_axes.description: Photo-ready crust vs safe set center
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: hierarchy: set and temp over color; tent if needed

conflict_axes.name: volume_max_vs_stability
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: stop short of instability; diagnose sinks before adding leavener

conflict_axes.name: minimal_mix_tenderness_vs_smooth_batter_aesthetics
conflict_axes.description: Lumpy tender muffins vs smooth overmixed batter

conflict_axes.name: foam_volume_vs_fold_thoroughness
conflict_axes.description: Protecting foam vs eliminating flour lumps
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: fold until just combined; accept tiny lumps over deflation

conflict_axes.name: recovery_attempt_vs_clean_restart
conflict_axes.description: Save the batch vs quality identity
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: recover only if actionable; disclose quality delta

conflict_axes.name: early_heat_spring_vs_crust_burn
conflict_axes.description: Strong spring heat vs exterior burn before center done
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: profile heat; tent; match to loaf mass

conflict_axes.name: hot_serve_intent_vs_cool_set_judgment
conflict_axes.description: Serve warm products vs evaluate after full cool
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: separate service intent from QC evaluation timing

conflict_axes.name: skewer_tradition_vs_thermometer
conflict_axes.description: Legacy toothpick rules vs numeric temp
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: temp ranks higher when target exists

edge_cases.description: Opening oven door early on a soufflé or angel food
edge_cases.mitigation: no door open until structure mostly set; use oven light; accept restart if collapsed

edge_cases.description: Molten chocolate cake judged by clean-skewer rule
edge_cases.mitigation: override clean-skewer; use time+edge set+known temp band for style

edge_cases.description: Cheesecake jiggle vs bread temp confusion
edge_cases.trigger: user applies bread doneness to custard cheese cake
edge_cases.mitigation: use jiggle band + cool set; not bread internal temps

edge_cases.description: Warm kitchen biscuit fat melts during cut-in
edge_cases.mitigation: chill flour/fat/bowl; pause chill; if already melted, restart for flaky style

edge_cases.description: Deep bundt dark exterior raw center
edge_cases.mitigation: lower temp, tent, extend; probe center; next time reduce depth or mass
if strength remains reshape and short reproof; else bake as flatbread-style or restart
warm slightly; beat in spoon of flour; adjust future egg temp/rate
yeast likely killed; restart with correct liquid temp band

edge_cases.description: Day-2 toughness from staling misread as overbake
edge_cases.trigger: fresh was fine, next day tough/dry
edge_cases.mitigation: advise storage/staling; refresh methods; do not only cut bake time

edge_cases.description: Convection oven running hot and fast
edge_cases.mitigation: reduce set temp 10-15 C; shorten prior time; rely on probe
usually terminal for full volume; bake as denser snack cake or restart foam

workflow.description: Temps, tools, leavener, pans, oven, order card
Choose method family and write order
workflow.gate: method matches fat state and product

workflow.description: Execute the chosen method (creaming, muffin, biscuit, sponge/foam, or knead path) with emulsion/foam/development controls and method-specific endpoints
workflow.artifact: mixed batter or dough at method endpoint
workflow.gate: method endpoint cues met without terminal failure

workflow.description: Temper eggs/chocolate/liquids when heat risks apply
workflow.gate: no thermal shock path left unchecked

workflow.description: Preheat, steam/score if needed, rack position
workflow.gate: oven at target before load for yeast goods

workflow.description: Monitor temp, skewer, touch, color in order
Pull at target adjusted for carryover
Cool per protocol; evaluate structure after set
If failure, diagnose, recover if actionable, update prevention

priority_rationale: Method and order come first; development and proof next; doneness hierarchy governs the bake; failure diagnosis and prevention close the loop.

dominance_rules.trigger: timer says done but cues disagree

dominance_rules.rationale: overmix toughness is worse than lumps
dominance_rules.trigger: urge to whisk muffin batter smooth

dominance_rules.action: run failure tree; change primary cause first

dominance_rules.rationale: save when quality-ok; restart when not
foam and custard failures are costly

iteration_protocol.action: run SUNK_CENTER tree; adjust bake, leaven, or proof accordingly
classify tight vs gummy; fix proof/development or set/hydration
reduce mix; verify muffin method endpoint
review grease, fold, door opens; usually restart
attempt EMULSION_NOTE recovery; fix temps next batch
check proof, development, oven spring prep
